title: Hyperparameter Optimization at Scale
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Hyperparameter Optimization at Scale ##### 11 days of GPU time to find nothing An AI team in Noida ran a grid search over a fine-tuning job: 4 learning rates × 3 batch sizes × 3 warmup ratios × 3 weight decays = 108 configurations, each taking roughly 2.5 GPU-hours. Total: 270 GPU-hours, about ₹1.1 lakh on their cloud contract, spread over 11 days. The best configuration beat their hand-picked baseline by 0.4%. The postmortem found two things. First, 70 of the 108 runs were visibly diverging by epoch 2 and still ran to completion — nobody had implemented pruning. Second, batch size and weight decay barely affected the metric at all, so 9 of every 12 runs were re-testing the same two meaningful dimensions with different irrelevant values. A 40-trial Optuna study with median pruning reproduced the best result in 22 GPU-hours. Hyperparameter optimization is not "try lots of things". It is a sequential decision problem, and treating it as one is worth an order of magnitude. ##### Grid, random, Bayesian **Grid search** evaluates the Cartesian product. Its fatal flaw is dimensional: with 6 hyperparameters at 4 values each, that is 4,096 trials. And Bergstra & Bengio's classic result shows that when only 2 of 6 dimensions matter, a grid of 4,096 trials tests each important dimension at only 4 distinct values — while 60 random trials test them at 60 distinct values each. **Random search** samples independently from distributions. It is embarrassingly parallel, needs no coordination, handles a mix of continuous and categorical parameters, and is a genuinely strong baseline. Its weakness is that it never learns: trial 300 is as uninformed as trial 1. **Bayesian optimization** builds a probabilistic model of the objective from completed trials and uses it to choose the next point. The loop: ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Evaluate a few random trials] --> B[Fit surrogate model of
score = f hyperparameters] B --> C[Acquisition function scores
every candidate point] C --> D[Pick candidate maximising
expected improvement] D --> E[Run the trial - expensive] E --> F[Add result to history] F --> B ``` The acquisition function is where the intelligence lives. Expected Improvement balances two things: regions where the surrogate predicts a high score (exploitation), and regions where the surrogate is uncertain (exploration). Pure exploitation gets stuck in a local optimum; pure exploration is random search. EI does both automatically, and it is why 40 informed trials can beat 400 random ones. Optuna's default sampler is **TPE** (Tree-structured Parzen Estimator), which inverts the usual formulation. Rather than modelling `p(score | params)` with a Gaussian process, it splits completed trials into a "good" set (top γ fraction) and a "bad" set, fits a density `l(x)` to each, and samples points maximising `l(x)/g(x)` — "likely under good trials, unlikely under bad ones". This scales far better than a GP to high dimensions and mixed parameter types, which is why Optuna uses it by default. ##### Optuna study design ```python import optuna, lightgbm as lgb from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score import numpy as np def objective(trial: optuna.Trial) -> float: params = { "objective": "binary", "verbosity": -1, # log-uniform for anything spanning orders of magnitude "learning_rate": trial.suggest_float("learning_rate", 5e-3, 0.3, log=True), "num_leaves": trial.suggest_int("num_leaves", 15, 255, log=True), "min_child_samples": trial.suggest_int("min_child_samples", 5, 200, log=True), "subsample": trial.suggest_float("subsample", 0.5, 1.0), "subsample_freq": 1, "colsample_bytree": trial.suggest_float("colsample_bytree", 0.4, 1.0), "reg_alpha": trial.suggest_float("reg_alpha", 1e-8, 10.0, log=True), "reg_lambda": trial.suggest_float("reg_lambda", 1e-8, 10.0, log=True), } # Conditional space: this parameter only exists for one branch params["boosting_type"] = trial.suggest_categorical("boosting_type", ["gbdt", "dart"]) if params["boosting_type"] == "dart": params["drop_rate"] = trial.suggest_float("drop_rate", 0.05, 0.3) scores = [] cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42) for fold, (tr, va) in enumerate(cv.split(X, y)): model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=3000, **params) model.fit(X.iloc[tr], y.iloc[tr], eval_set=[(X.iloc[va], y.iloc[va])], eval_metric="average_precision", callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(100, verbose=False)]) p = model.predict_proba(X.iloc[va])[:, 1] scores.append(average_precision_score(y.iloc[va], p)) trial.report(float(np.mean(scores)), step=fold) # enable fold-level pruning if trial.should_prune(): raise optuna.TrialPruned() trial.set_user_attr("std", float(np.std(scores))) return float(np.mean(scores)) study = optuna.create_study( direction="maximize", study_name="fraud_lgbm_v3", storage="postgresql://optuna@db:5432/optuna", # enables distributed + resume load_if_exists=True, sampler=optuna.samplers.TPESampler(seed=42, n_startup_trials=20, multivariate=True), pruner=optuna.pruners.MedianPruner(n_startup_trials=10, n_warmup_steps=2), ) study.optimize(objective, n_trials=200, timeout=3600 * 6, n_jobs=1) ``` Design decisions worth calling out: - **`log=True` for scale-spanning parameters.** Learning rate 0.001 → 0.01 is the same *relative* jump as 0.01 → 0.1. Uniform sampling would put 90% of samples in the top decade. - **`n_startup_trials`** controls how long TPE samples randomly before modelling. Too few and the surrogate is built on noise; 10–20 is standard. - **`multivariate=True`** lets TPE model parameter interactions instead of treating each dimension independently. Usually a clear improvement. - **Persistent storage** turns the study into a resumable, shareable, distributed object. - **Conditional parameters** are Optuna's structural advantage: the search space is defined by Python control flow, so `drop_rate` simply does not exist in gbdt trials. Grid search cannot express this. ##### Pruning: the biggest single win Pruning kills trials that are clearly losing, freeing compute for promising ones. On deep learning this is frequently a 3–10× speedup. ```python from optuna.integration import PyTorchLightningPruningCallback def objective(trial): lr = trial.suggest_float("lr", 1e-5, 1e-2, log=True) model = build_model(lr=lr, dropout=trial.suggest_float("dropout", 0.0, 0.5)) for epoch in range(30): train_one_epoch(model) val_auc = evaluate(model) trial.report(val_auc, step=epoch) if trial.should_prune(): # cuts losers at epoch 2-3 raise optuna.TrialPruned() return val_auc ``` | Pruner | Rule | Best for | |---|---|---| | `MedianPruner` | Prune if below median of prior trials at this step | Safe default | | `SuccessiveHalvingPruner` | ASHA: allocate budget in rungs, promote top 1/η | Massively parallel | | `HyperbandPruner` | Runs SHA across multiple budget schedules | Unknown budget/quality trade-off | | `PercentilePruner` | Configurable percentile threshold | Tuning aggressiveness | | `PatientPruner` | Wraps another, adds patience | Noisy curves | **Successive halving** is the core idea: start N configurations with a small budget, keep the top 1/η, give survivors η× more budget, repeat. **Hyperband** wraps SHA in an outer loop over different initial budgets, hedging against the failure mode where a slow-starting configuration is the eventual winner — a real risk when comparing learning rates, since a low LR looks bad early and wins late. Set `n_warmup_steps` high enough to survive warmup epochs, or you will prune every configuration using a learning-rate warmup schedule. ##### Multi-objective optimization Production models trade off accuracy against latency, size and cost. Optimising a weighted sum forces you to pick the weights before you know the trade-off curve. Pareto optimisation shows you the curve instead. ```python def objective(trial): n_layers = trial.suggest_int("n_layers", 1, 6) width = trial.suggest_categorical("width", [64, 128, 256, 512]) model = build(n_layers, width) auc = train_and_eval(model) latency_ms = measure_p99_latency(model, n=500) return auc, latency_ms study = optuna.create_study( directions=["maximize", "minimize"], sampler=optuna.samplers.NSGAIISampler(seed=42), # or TPESampler for MO ) study.optimize(objective, n_trials=300) for t in study.best_trials: # the Pareto front print(f"AUC {t.values[0]:.4f} p99 {t.values[1]:.1f}ms {t.params}") optuna.visualization.plot_pareto_front(study, target_names=["AUC", "p99 ms"]).show() ``` The Pareto front is the set of trials where you cannot improve one objective without worsening another. Handing a product owner a front — "0.912 AUC at 40 ms, or 0.918 at 190 ms" — is a far better conversation than handing them one number. Note that pruning does not apply to multi-objective studies, and NSGA-II needs more trials than TPE because it is an evolutionary method. ##### Distributed HPO Because Optuna stores trials in a database, distribution is close to trivial: run the same script on N machines pointing at the same storage. ```bash # Any number of workers, any machines, same command for i in $(seq 1 8); do optuna study optimize tune.py objective \ --study-name fraud_lgbm_v3 \ --storage postgresql://optuna@db:5432/optuna \ --n-trials 25 & done ``` Use PostgreSQL or MySQL for real parallelism — SQLite locks under concurrent writes and will corrupt long studies. On Kubernetes, run workers as a `Job` with `parallelism: 8`. Ray Tune is the alternative when you need fault-tolerant scheduling, GPU-aware placement and population-based training; Optuna is simpler and integrates with Ray if you want TPE inside Ray's scheduler. One subtlety of parallelism: with 8 concurrent workers, TPE proposes trials before seeing the other 7 results, so the effective sequential advantage shrinks. Beyond ~16 workers, ASHA-style pruning contributes more than sampler intelligence. ##### Analysing the study The optimisation output is not just `best_params`. ```python print(study.best_value, study.best_params) print(optuna.importance.get_param_importances(study)) # fANOVA-based optuna.visualization.plot_optimization_history(study) # is it still improving? optuna.visualization.plot_param_importances(study) # which dims matter optuna.visualization.plot_slice(study) # marginal effect per param optuna.visualization.plot_contour(study, params=["learning_rate", "num_leaves"]) ``` Parameter importances tell you what to drop from the next study — exactly the analysis the Noida team never ran. If the optimisation history is still climbing at trial 200, you stopped too early. If the best trial's CV standard deviation is large, you may have optimised into noise; check the top 10 trials and prefer a configuration in a broad, stable region over a lone spike. Finally: the tuned score on the CV folds is optimistically biased, because you selected on it across 200 trials. Report the final number on a test set the study never touched. ##### Common mistakes - Grid search in more than 3 dimensions. - Uniform sampling of learning rate or regularization strength instead of log-uniform. - No pruner, so hopeless trials consume the entire budget. - `n_warmup_steps` too low, pruning every trial that uses LR warmup. - SQLite storage with parallel workers. - Tuning on the same split used for early stopping, then reporting that score. - Ranges too narrow — the optimum sits on a boundary and nobody notices. - Ignoring `plot_param_importances` and re-tuning irrelevant parameters forever. - Optimising a weighted sum when a Pareto front was the real question. - Spending 300 trials on hyperparameters when one new feature would have moved the metric more. ##### Hands-on Tune the same model twice under an identical wall-clock budget: once with `RandomSampler` and no pruner, once with `TPESampler` plus `MedianPruner`. Plot both optimisation histories on one axis and report best score, trial count, and pruned-trial count. Then run `get_param_importances` and identify which two dimensions actually mattered. For the mini-project, build a reusable HPO harness: a config-driven search-space definition, pluggable sampler and pruner, PostgreSQL storage for resume and distribution, MLflow or W&B logging of every trial, multi-objective support returning `(metric, latency)`, and a CLI that runs `tune`, `resume` and `report`. Test it on two different model families to prove it is genuinely reusable. Then write your explanation of how Bayesian optimization finds good configurations in fewer trials — surrogate, acquisition function, exploration/exploitation — and describe precisely what a sampler does in Optuna versus what a pruner does. ##### Key takeaways - Grid search wastes budget re-testing dimensions that do not matter; random search is a strong baseline, Bayesian is better. - A sampler decides *where* to look next by fitting a surrogate and maximising expected improvement; TPE does this with density ratios. - Pruning is usually the single largest speedup available — report intermediate values and let the pruner kill losers early. - Persistent DB storage makes an Optuna study resumable, distributed and analysable; never use SQLite for parallel workers. - Read parameter importances and the optimisation history; the study's real output is understanding, not just `best_params`.
